- 🔬 What can WarpX and ImpactX reveal about plasmas and particle beams?
- 🧩 How do particles, grid cells, and simulation steps turn into computing work?
- 🚀 How do we launch, measure, and explore a simulation on a remote CPU or GPU?

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: objectives

- 💡 Connect each physical system to the numerical model used by the code.
- 🚀 Run a small WarpX example and a 3D wakefield example on GPU.
- ⏱️ Read simulation logs and tell physical simulation time apart from elapsed runtime.
- 📊 Visualize plasma dynamics and beam transport using saved diagnostics.
- 🔍 Measure what changes when we track more particles in ImpactX.

## Your route through the tutorial 🗺️

Today you will make electron streams form a wave, launch a laser into a
plasma, and send a beam through magnets. Along the way, keep an eye on what
the computer is doing: how long it takes, which hardware is working, and
how much data it saves. 🔬 💻

Read [Introduction to WarpX](introduction.Rmd) for the particle-in-cell
(PIC) method and the physical questions WarpX can help answer. Read
[Introduction to ImpactX](introduction-impactx.Rmd) for beam dynamics,
accelerator elements, and the questions ImpactX can help answer. These pages
provide the background for the slides and remain available after the workshop.
You do not need to derive the equations or write a simulation from scratch.

Our three stops connect the physics to the computing:

| Example | Physical system and numerical model | Computing activity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 🎢 Two-stream instability | Two electron populations interacting through fields on a 1D grid | Practice running WarpX, reading its log, and plotting output |
| 🏄 Laser wakefield | A laser and plasma evolving on a 3D grid with computational particles | Run on a CPU and GPU; connect grid size, time steps, and diagnostics to cost |
| 🧲 HTU beam transport | A bunch of electrons tracked through a sequence of magnets | Run on CPU and GPU; compare particle counts, runtime, output size, and beam plots |

The wakefield and transport examples illustrate two stages of an accelerator:
creating an energetic beam in plasma and transporting it through magnets.
They run independently here, although in principle WarpX can supply the incoming ImpactX bunch.

## Meet your remote machine 💻

Registered participants receive an AWS-hosted JupyterLab link through Slack.
Open that link; the software and tutorial files are already installed.
Your browser is the interface: the simulation and its files live on the
remote machine.

Start by finding out where you landed. Open **File > New > Terminal** in
JupyterLab and run:

```bash
cd ~/warpx-tutorials/episodes/files/llnl-hpc-2026
pwd
lscpu
nvidia-smi
```

`pwd` shows the working directory. `lscpu` describes the CPU; `nvidia-smi`
shows the NVIDIA GPU and its memory. Record the CPU and GPU models so your
runtime measurements have context. Available resources may be shared with
other work on the instance.

📝 Keep a small run record as you go: **hardware, input settings, elapsed
time, output size, and one observation from the plots**. Those notes will
help you explain differences between runs.

The hosted image provides two Python environments:

| Where you work | CPU | GPU |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jupyter notebook: **Kernel > Change Kernel** | **WarpX CPU** | **WarpX GPU** |
| Terminal activation command | `source /opt/venv-cpu/bin/activate` | `source /opt/venv-gpu/bin/activate` |

💡 **Two places to choose your environment:** both environments include
ImpactX as well as WarpX. Selecting a notebook kernel does **not** change
the environment in an already open terminal.
For the exercises below, run WarpX from the terminal and analyze its output
in notebooks. The ImpactX notebook launches its own simulation processes.
Before repeating a WarpX exercise, preserve its completed `diags/` folder
and `run.log` under new, unused names; the drivers reuse those output paths.

### Joining from your own machine? 🏠

Follow the [Docker or Conda setup instructions](./files/llnl-hpc-2026/README.md)
before continuing. Keep the complete tutorial folder together. The `/opt/venv-*`
activation commands apply to the hosted image and Docker; use your installed
environment on other systems. The 3D exercise requires a GPU-enabled WarpX
build to use the GPU. CPU execution is possible but can take substantially

## Exercise 1: run and inspect a two-stream simulation

🎢 Start with two electron populations moving in opposite directions at one tenth of the
speed of light. Small density variations create an electric field, which
changes the electron motion and can make those variations grow. This
feedback is the **two-stream instability**. Eventually particles become
trapped in the wave and the rapid growth levels off.

WarpX follows this interaction along one spatial direction, **z**, on a
periodic grid: particles leaving one end re-enter at the other. A stationary
positive background is assumed; ions are not tracked explicitly. This small
example introduces the same particle–field update cycle used in the larger
wakefield calculation.

### Launch your first run 🚀

Your first run is ready to go. From the tutorial directory in the terminal:

```bash
source /opt/venv-cpu/bin/activate
cd two_stream_instability
ls
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=2
time python run_two_stream_instability.py > run.log 2>&1
```

The [Python driver](./files/llnl-hpc-2026/two_stream_instability/run_two_stream_instability.py)
loads the [input file](./files/llnl-hpc-2026/two_stream_instability/two_stream_instability_input.txt)
and starts WarpX. `OMP_NUM_THREADS=2` requests two CPU threads where the
build uses OpenMP. `time` reports elapsed time as **real**; `user` and `sys`
are CPU accounting times. The simulation's messages are saved in `run.log`.
A quiet terminal is expected here: the messages are going to the file.
Wait for the terminal prompt to return before running the next commands.

```bash
tail -n 30 run.log
du -sh diags
```

`tail` displays the end of the log; check for normal completion rather than
assuming that a returned prompt means success. `du` reports the disk space
used by the saved diagnostics. Record elapsed time and output size. Runtime
depends on the machine; this is the short warm-up, not a performance benchmark.

### Peek under the hood 🔧

Open the input file in JupyterLab's editor and find the settings below.
You do not need to decipher every line: first locate the grid, particles,
and output controls. Keep their values unchanged for this run.

| Setting | Meaning in this run |
| --- | --- |
| `geometry.dims = 1` | Fields vary along one spatial direction |
| `my_constants.nx = 256` | The domain has 256 grid cells |
| `ele1.num_particles_per_cell = 200` and the equivalent `ele2` setting | Each cell initially samples each electron population with 200 macroparticles |
| `stop_time = T` | End at the specified physical simulation time |
| `particles.intervals` | How often particle snapshots are written |

That little input describes 256 × 200 × 2 = **102,400 macroparticles**. They
represent many more physical electrons. At each step, WarpX updates particle
motion and fields; writing a snapshot adds a separate output operation.

### Spot the instability 📈

Open [two_stream_instability_plots.ipynb](./files/llnl-hpc-2026/two_stream_instability/two_stream_instability_plots.ipynb)
from the `two_stream_instability` folder and select **WarpX CPU**. Run its
cells after the simulation finishes.

A **phase-space plot** shows position on one axis and momentum on the other.
Here they are z and longitudinal momentum divided by the electron mass and
the speed of light. The initially separate streams bend and roll into loops
as particles become trapped in the wave. These are loops in position–momentum
space, not circular paths in the simulation box.

![Example phase space from the related two-stream lesson.](https://gist.github.com/user-attachments/assets/0160a10a-9a08-443c-84a3-610a9a5eeb73){alt="Two electron streams roll into loops in position–momentum space as particles become trapped in a wave."}

This reference image comes from the [two-stream lesson](a-two-stream-instability.Rmd);
your run can differ in fine detail. The notebook also plots field energy over
**physical time**. Look for the electric field energy to rise and then level
off. This time axis describes the plasma's evolution, not how long the
computer ran.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: challenge

### Checkpoint: follow the evidence 🕵️

Find the loops in phase space and the rise in electric field energy. Can
you identify evidence of the instability in both plots?

Then point to the input file, execution log, particle output, and analysis
notebook. You now have the four parts of a simulation workflow—and will
use them again in the next exercise.

## Exercise 2: run a 3D laser wakefield on a GPU

🏄 Next stop: a laser-driven plasma wave. Read the [Laser-Wakefield Acceleration lesson](a-laser-wakefield.Rmd) for
the laser–plasma setup, numerical representation, and interpretation of the
plots. In this example a laser drives a plasma wave whose electric field can
accelerate electrons; WarpX evolves the particles and fields on a 3D grid.
Now put the hosted GPU to work and measure what it takes to produce those
wakefield pictures.

**AWS participants: keep working in `llnl-hpc-2026/htu/`.** The workshop
and the wakefield lesson use the same input, Python driver, notebook, and
shared helper script in this folder.

### Launch the laser and watch the GPU 🔦

In the terminal, navigate to the wakefield directory and activate the GPU
environment explicitly:

```bash
cd ~/warpx-tutorials/episodes/files/llnl-hpc-2026/htu/lwfa_warpx
source /opt/venv-gpu/bin/activate
time python run_lwfa_warpx.py > run.log 2>&1
```

This uses the [driver](./files/llnl-hpc-2026/htu/lwfa_warpx/run_lwfa_warpx.py)
and [input](./files/llnl-hpc-2026/htu/lwfa_warpx/lwfa_warpx_input.txt) in that
directory. In a **second terminal**, inspect progress while it runs:

```bash
cd ~/warpx-tutorials/episodes/files/llnl-hpc-2026/htu/lwfa_warpx
tail -n 20 run.log
nvidia-smi
```

⏱️ Follow the log's step count, physical time, and step timings as the run advances. GPU memory use
and utilization in `nvidia-smi` are snapshots; a single observation is not
a peak-memory measurement or an average utilization. The completed reference
run took about **8 minutes 25 seconds** on an RTX A2000 8 GB laptop GPU;
this is context, not an expected time on your instance.

Once the run finishes, record the elapsed time and output size:

```bash
tail -n 30 run.log
du -sh diags
```

The driver uses the same `diags/` location each time. Before repeating a run,
preserve the output and log under new names, for example `diags-baseline`
and `run-baseline.log`, using JupyterLab's file browser. Do this only after
the run finishes, and choose unused names.

### Tiny physics, plenty of computing 🧩

The input uses **32 × 32 × 512 = 524,288 grid cells** in a moving box
16 × 16 × 20 µm in size. The longitudinal spacing is about 0.039 µm,
which samples the 0.8 µm laser wavelength with about 20 cells. There is one
initial macroparticle per cell per species where plasma is loaded; electrons
move while helium ions stay fixed. The moving window follows the laser,
limiting the volume that must be simulated at once.

The time step is approximately **0.129 femtoseconds**, with **1,836 steps**
in the default run. A femtosecond is one millionth of a billionth of a second.
Resolving these short physical scales requires many repeated grid and particle
updates. The GPU executes many of those similar operations concurrently.

💭 While the GPU works, try a cost estimate on paper. Imagine halving the
spacing in **all three directions**
while keeping the physical box, duration, and particles per cell fixed.
There would be eight times as many cells and approximately eight times as
many particles. With this solver's time-step constraint, approximately twice
as many steps would also be needed. That suggests about sixteen times the
update work, before communication and output effects. It is not a measured
runtime prediction; do not launch that larger case during this exercise.

### Find the wake 🏄

Open [wakefield.ipynb](./files/llnl-hpc-2026/htu/wakefield.ipynb) from the
`htu` folder. The notebook analyzes the terminal run; it does not launch it.
Its default `out_folder = "lwfa_warpx/diags/diag1"` matches the output above.
The hosted **WarpX GPU** kernel includes the analysis packages; plotting the
saved output itself does not require GPU acceleration.

Use the [standalone lesson's plot guide](a-laser-wakefield.Rmd#interpret-the-results)
to identify the electron-depleted cavity, the accelerating field, and the
energy distribution. Both copies of the example use the same physical and
numerical settings. Inspect a snapshot during propagation; the final frame
is after the moving window has left the plasma.

📸 The default takes a snapshot every **200 steps** and at the end. This
connects an HPC choice to what you can learn: sparse output saves disk space,
but you cannot inspect an unsaved stage of the wake. Full field and particle
snapshots are more expensive to store than a few reduced quantities, such
as the field-energy history in the warm-up.

If time permits, try taking fewer snapshots: preserve the baseline output,
change only `diag1.intervals` from `200` to `400`, and rerun. Compare elapsed
time, disk use, and the available snapshots. Which stages of the wake can
you still inspect? The physics settings are unchanged, but the history is
sampled less frequently. Do not expect total runtime to halve: computation
still proceeds through every step. For an optional physics variation, change
only `a0`, the laser strength, and compare the wake at the same saved step.

## Exercise 3: track the HTU beam with ImpactX

🧲 Once a beam is created, the magnets take over: we need to steer and focus it.
Here an independent, computer-generated electron bunch passes through the
**Hundred Terawatt Undulator (HTU)** beamline. We use the
[upstream HTU example](https://impactx.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage/examples/htu_beamline/README.html)
with **100 MeV total energy** and **25 pC charge**. MeV is a unit of particle
energy and pC is a unit of electric charge; total energy includes the
approximately 0.511 MeV electron rest energy.

Quadrupole magnets focus the beam, and a sequence of bending magnets called
a **chicane** takes it along a sideways detour. ImpactX advances particles
through the mathematical models of these components. **Space charge is off**:
particles respond to the prescribed magnets without interacting through
their own fields. This run therefore does not repeat the plasma field solve
used in the WarpX example.

### Run the beam transport simulation 🧲

Open [htu_transport.ipynb](./files/llnl-hpc-2026/htu/htu_transport.ipynb) from
`htu/` and select **WarpX CPU**. The setup cell exposes these settings:

```python
particles = 10000
total_energies_MeV = [100]
chicane_r56_um = 200.0
```

Keep these defaults for your first HTU run and run notebook steps 1–3. The notebook calls the
[shared helper script](./files/llnl-hpc-2026/htu/tutorial_helpers.py), which
contains the HTU lattice, source, simulation setup, and plotting functions.
It creates a fresh run folder, saves a log, and reports elapsed runtime and
the size of the simulation output. The measured time includes process
startup, tracking, and writing diagnostics; notebook plotting is excluded.
Measurements are also saved in `performance.json`.

### Explore the beam screens 🔍

Press **Play screens** in the notebook or drag the slider to follow the bunch.
Find the first focusing screen (`TCPhosphor`), the middle of the chicane
(`ChicaneSlit`), and the exit. Does the beam stay round?


The maps look across the beam, perpendicular to its direction of travel.
Turn off **Zoom to fit** to compare snapshots on fixed axes. With zoom on,
read the units: a similar-looking spot may be micrometers or millimeters
across. Color shows charge per bin; changing bin areas means color alone
does not compare physical density per unit area. The saved `beam_explorer.html`
also opens directly in a browser.

![Horizontal and vertical beam sizes along HTU.](./files/llnl-hpc-2026/htu/images/htu-transmission.png){alt="Horizontal and vertical rms beam sizes versus distance, with screen landmarks identifying focusing, the chicane, and the undulator."}

Follow x and y separately. Their **rms sizes** measure the spread of particle
positions around their means. Where is the beam narrowest in each plane?
Can you find a matching screen in the viewer?

The **lattice strip** below the curves places the magnets and screens on the
same distance axis. Use it to connect beam focusing and expansion to the
nearby elements. Gaps are drifts. Element lengths are to scale; symbol
heights represent neither the beam size nor a physical aperture. Symbols
also include magnets whose field is set to zero.

The lattice has no modeled apertures. The notebook prints a remaining-charge
check, but that does not prove a real beam fits through every opening.
Invalid tracking is flagged and affected curves stop; numerical failure is
not interpreted as physical beam loss.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: challenge

### Ten times the particles—what changes? 🔍

Make a prediction first: which will change most visibly—the beam-size curve,
the detail in the density maps, or the amount of data saved?

Run notebook **step 4**. It launches a second simulation with ten times as
many particles, keeping the energy, magnets, and thread setting fixed. Two
bar charts compare runtime and output size; the next cells show the new
beam maps and beam-size curves. Both runs remain in separate folders.

| Run | Macroparticles | Elapsed time (s) | Output (MiB) | Observation about the beam plots |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | 10,000 | | | |
| More particles | 100,000 | | | |

The physical bunch charge remains **25 pC**: each macroparticle represents
a smaller share of it. This changes the sampling of the same beam model,
not the physical number of electrons in the bunch. Compare the beam-size
curves and the detail in the density maps as well as the cost. More samples
do not correct missing physics or guarantee that all numerical errors are small.

Ten times as many particles means more tracking work and particle output,
but total runtime need not increase by ten. Startup, file operations, and
other fixed costs can be significant in a small run. This is a workload-size
comparison on fixed hardware, not a parallel scaling measurement.

Compare your measurements with your prediction. If the runtime did not grow
tenfold, which parts of the run might account for the difference?

### Optional: change the beam energy

Return to `particles = 10000`. Set `total_energies_MeV = [100, 150]` and
`chicane_r56_um = 0.0`, then rerun the settings cell and **steps 1–3 only**. Both beams now use
zero chicane field, following the upstream off-energy example. Compare the
horizontal and vertical beam sizes at equal distances.

The magnets and 100 MeV reference stay fixed. The 150 MeV case shifts the
mean energy while preserving sampled positions and absolute momentum
spreads; its initial angular divergence and relative energy spread are
therefore smaller. The shared helper script records the conventions and upstream provenance.

## From this instance to a supercomputer 🌍

You have now run two codes and explored three physical systems. The
warm-up, wakefield, and HTU runs use different physical models and
workloads. Their times cannot establish a CPU-to-GPU speedup. For that,
you would run the **same input and diagnostics** on each device and record
the hardware, software, initialization costs, and repeated timings.

A compute **node** is one machine, with CPU cores, memory, and possibly GPUs.
On larger installations, MPI processes divide work across nodes and exchange
data. This introduces communication and workload-distribution costs as well
as more computing capacity. The tutorial container is built without MPI;
these exercises run on one node and do not demonstrate multi-node scaling.
On a scheduled cluster, simulations run on allocated compute nodes, using
the site's job-submission instructions, rather than on its login node.

## Keep exploring: connect the codes 🔗

A larger study can pass a plasma-generated bunch from WarpX to ImpactX.
That requires a resolved source, a suitable particle selection, and consistent
coordinate conventions. It is outside these exercises: a high-energy tail alone does not establish
a usable beam. The two notebooks use independent sources.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: keypoints

- 🧩 Physics and numerical representation determine the workload; hardware
  determines how that workload is executed.
- 📝 Record the input, hardware, elapsed runtime, and output alongside the plots.
- 💾 More particles, finer grids, and more frequent diagnostics have different
  scientific benefits and computational costs.
- 🔍 Compare the same problem to measure a hardware speedup; compare physical
  observables to judge whether a numerical change matters scientifically.
